meta.title: Who really said "A dream you dream alone is only a dream. A dream you dream together is reality"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not John Lennon. The line is Yoko Ono's — an idea she put in print in 1964 and sang in 1972. Lennon only quoted it, from memory and imprecisely.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A dream you dream alone is only a dream. A dream you dream together is reality'?
meta.ogDescription: Yoko Ono wrote it — in "Grapefruit" (1964), then in her song "Now or Never" (1972). John Lennon quoted it in David Sheff's interviews, and quote sites have credited him ever since.

answer.label: Not John Lennon — actually Yoko Ono
answer.authorDates: b. 18 February 1933 · Japanese artist, musician and peace activist
answer.sourceLine: The words are Yoko Ono’s, and she had been writing them since 1964: “Six Film Scripts” (Tokyo, June 1964), published in Grapefruit, gives the thought as “A dream you dream alone may be a dream, but a dream two people dream together is a reality.” The popular wording is closest to her song “Now or Never,” issued as a US single on 13 November 1972 and collected on Approximately Infinite Universe on 8 January 1973, whose lyric carries the credit “© Ono Music, Inc., 1972”; biographer John Blaney writes that Ono would later paraphrase that song’s main idea with the aphorism. Either way the line is hers — Lennon’s only documented connection to it is quoting her, from memory and imprecisely.

source.excerpt: A dream you dream alone is only a dream. A dream you dream together is reality.
trail: June 1964 — Ono writes “Six Film Scripts” in Tokyo, published in Grapefruit the same year. The aphorism is already there, in an earlier phrasing: “A dream you dream alone may be a dream, but a dream two people dream together is a reality” — the wording her own official channel still gives, and the wording books quote as “— Yoko Ono, Grapefruit” (Open Library, search inside ↗).
1972 — Ono writes “Now or Never”; the lyric is credited “© Ono Music, Inc., 1972” in the lyric-permissions credits of her book John Lennon: Summer of 1980 (1983) (Open Library, search inside ↗).
13 November 1972 — the song is issued as a US single backed by “Move on Fast,” then collected on Approximately Infinite Universe on 8 January 1973 (Wikipedia ↗).

December 1980 — Wikiquote’s sourced entry records Lennon quoting the line, citing David Sheff’s All We Are Saying, p. 16 (Wikiquote ↗). In the book’s text it is quoted from memory and broken off — “you’ll have to look it up” (Open Library, search inside ↗).
31 March 1994 — in the New York Times, critic Stephen Holden describes the line as expressing a “Beatles-style utopianism,” placing it squarely in Ono’s song (Wikipedia ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the prose form Wikiquote lists under Ono’s name, and the form biographer John Blaney says Ono used to paraphrase the song. On the record itself the couplet is sung slightly differently — the second line runs “dream we dream together” (lyric transcription ↗).

author.name: Yoko Ono
author.heading: About Yoko Ono
author.metaLine: b. 18 February 1933 · Japanese artist, musician and peace activist
author.bio: Yoko Ono is a Japanese artist, musician and peace activist whose work also takes in performance art and filmmaking. John Lennon first became familiar with her and her work at her November 1966 Indica Gallery exhibition, where the piece “Ceiling Painting” rewarded a climb up a white ladder with a single word: YES. Approximately Infinite Universe (1973), her third solo album, turned from the avant-garde rock of her first two records toward a more conventional pop/rock sound — and it is on that album that this sentence lives.

cite.sourceCitation: Yoko Ono, “Now or Never,” single (Apple, 13 November 1972), collected on Approximately Infinite Universe (Apple, 8 January 1973); lyric credited “© Ono Music, Inc., 1972.” An earlier phrasing of the same aphorism appears in Ono’s “Six Film Scripts” (Tokyo, June 1964), published in Grapefruit; biographer John Blaney writes that the familiar prose form is Ono’s own paraphrase of the song. Lennon quoted the line in David Sheff, All We Are Saying: The Last Major Interview with John Lennon and Yoko Ono (St. Martin’s Griffin, 2000), 16 — per Wikiquote’s sourced entry. Not a John Lennon quotation.

misattribution.heading: A line by Ono, filed under Lennon
misattribution.intro: Search the sentence and almost every result says John Lennon. The credit is wrong in a specific, traceable way: the words are Yoko Ono’s, and Lennon’s only documented contact with them is quoting his wife — badly.

items.why: Goodreads files the exact wording under Lennon’s name with no source (Goodreads ↗), and it reaches print the same way: Preston Bailey’s Celebrations opens its acknowledgments “John Lennon once said…” before the quotation (Open Library, search inside ↗). Wikiquote’s John Lennon article carries no entry for the line in any section (Wikiquote ↗).

The sung couplet is not quite the quotable prose everyone repeats: on the record the second line runs “dream we dream together” (lyric transcription ↗), and Lennon biographer John Blaney writes that Ono “would paraphrase the song’s main idea with the aphorism” in its familiar form (Open Library, search inside ↗). The polished sentence is Ono’s own restatement, not the lyric verbatim.

Wikiquote records Lennon quoting the line in the Sheff interviews (Wikiquote ↗). In the book’s own text it is reached for and left unfinished — “I don’t know, you’ll have to look it up” — followed by “A dream you dream alone is one thing, a dream you dream together…” (Open Library, search inside ↗). Quoting a line is not writing it.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Yoko Ono’s. Wikiquote lists them under her name as “a line written by Ono many years before, and quoted by Lennon in December 1980” (Wikiquote ↗) without naming the year or the work. Ono’s own official channel dates the thought to “Six Film Scripts” (Tokyo, June 1964), published in Grapefruit; the familiar wording is the one that belongs to her 1972 song “Now or Never.”

context.heading: Why the credit slid from Ono to Lennon
lead: “Now or Never” is a protest song, not a love song. Ono wrote it, Lennon played guitar on it, and the two co-produced the record; the single’s sleeve carried photographs of Vietnamese victims of the My Lai massacre, and Cash Box reviewed it as “a delicate social commentary” (Wikipedia ↗). The dream couplet is where the argument lands: the change she is demanding only counts if enough people want it at the same time.

How the credit moved is easy to reconstruct. Lennon reached for his wife’s line in the long interview David Sheff published as The Playboy Interviews with John Lennon and Yōko Ono, later reissued as All We Are Saying — and that book is the citation Wikiquote gives for the quotation (Wikiquote ↗). From a famous man quoting a line in a famous interview, it is one short step to a quotation card that reads simply “— John Lennon.”
context.detailsSummary: What the interview text actually shows
detailsBody: Searching inside both editions of the Sheff interviews turns the line up in a strikingly unsure form: “…you’ll have to look it up. ‘A dream you dream alone is one thing, a dream you dream together…’” (Open Library, search inside ↗). That is not an author delivering an aphorism; it is someone trying to recall one.

Wikiquote’s sourced entry names the speaker as Lennon, dates the moment to December 1980 and cites All We Are Saying at page 16 (Wikiquote ↗). The Internet Archive’s scan of that book is lending-restricted, so we could not open page 16 ourselves — the page number rests on Wikiquote, while the presence of the passage in the book is independently confirmed by full-text search.
context.pull: Lennon quoted it. Ono wrote it.
